questions.q: Which nerves supply the detrusor muscle?
questions.explain: Parasympathetic stimulation contracts the detrusor and empties the bladder.

open.q: Which nerves supply the detrusor muscle?

questions.q: Which nerve supplies the external urethral sphincter?
questions.explain: It carries somatic motor fibres from S2–S4 (Onuf's nucleus).

open.q: Which nerve supplies the external urethral sphincter?

questions.q: What kind of muscle forms the external urethral sphincter, and is it voluntary?
questions.explain: This voluntary sphincter lets you delay micturition.

open.q: What kind of muscle forms the external urethral sphincter, and is it voluntary?

questions.q: Which spinal cord segments contain the centre for the micturition reflex?
questions.explain: The reflex is integrated in the sacral cord and modified by higher centres.

open.q: Which spinal cord segments contain the centre for the micturition reflex?

questions.q: At about what bladder volume does a strong urge to void usually arise?
questions.explain: The first sensation is at about 150 ml. Capacity is about 400–500 ml.

open.q: At about what bladder volume does a strong urge to void usually arise?

questions.q: What does sympathetic stimulation (hypogastric nerve) do to the detrusor and internal sphincter?
options: Contracts the detrusor and relaxes the sphincter
Relaxes the detrusor and contracts the internal sphincter
Has no effect on the bladder
questions.explain: This promotes storage of urine.

open.q: What does sympathetic stimulation (hypogastric nerve) do to the detrusor and internal sphincter?

questions.q: What kind of reflex is micturition, and what modifies it?
options: A reflex controlled only by the cerebellum
A spinal reflex modulated by higher centres
questions.explain: The pons, hypothalamus and cortex facilitate or inhibit the sacral reflex.

open.q: What kind of reflex is micturition, and what modifies it?
accept: spinal reflex modified by higher centres

questions.q: What does the pontine micturition centre do?
options: Stores urine by relaxing detrusor only
Coordinates detrusor contraction with sphincter relaxation
questions.explain: Damage above the pons disturbs voluntary control, while damage below it disturbs coordination.

open.q: What does the pontine micturition centre do?
accept: coordinates detrusor contraction and sphincter relaxation

questions.q: What happens to the bladder after spinal cord transection above the sacral segments?
options: Initial retention during spinal shock, then automatic reflex emptying
questions.explain: The sacral reflex returns after weeks, but without voluntary control.

open.q: What happens to the bladder after spinal cord transection above the sacral segments?

questions.q: What results from destruction of the sacral cord or the sensory nerves of the bladder?
questions.explain: There is no reflex contraction, so the bladder fills until urine overflows.

open.q: What results from destruction of the sacral cord or the sensory nerves of the bladder?

questions.q: What does a cystometrogram plot?
questions.explain: The curve shows a flat phase of accommodation and then a sharp rise at micturition.

open.q: What does a cystometrogram plot?

questions.q: What three openings mark the corners of the bladder trigone?
options: The two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice
The two ureteric orifices and the external urethral meatus
The urachus and the two ureteric orifices
The internal and external urethral orifices and the urachus
questions.explain: The trigone is the smooth triangular area at the base of the bladder.

open.q: What three openings mark the corners of the bladder trigone?
accept: two ureteric orifices and internal urethral orifice

questions.q: How much residual urine remains in the bladder after a normal micturition?
questions.explain: A significant residual volume suggests obstruction or a neurogenic bladder.

open.q: How much residual urine remains in the bladder after a normal micturition?

questions.q: At about what bladder volume is the first sensation of filling usually felt?
questions.explain: The first desire to void follows at about 150 to 250 mL.

open.q: At about what bladder volume is the first sensation of filling usually felt?

questions.q: At about what bladder volume does the first desire to void arise?
questions.explain: Between 300 and 400 mL the micturition reflex begins and the bladder feels uncomfortably full.

open.q: At about what bladder volume does the first desire to void arise?

questions.q: At roughly what volume do pain and loss of control occur?
questions.explain: Above the normal capacity, wall tension causes pain and voluntary control fails.

open.q: At roughly what volume do pain and loss of control occur?

questions.q: About how long are the female and the male urethra?
options: About 4 cm in females and about 20 cm in males
About 2 cm in females and 8 cm in males
About 20 cm in females and 4 cm in males
About 10 cm in females and 30 cm in males
questions.explain: The short female urethra makes urinary infections more common in women.

open.q: About how long are the female and the male urethra?

questions.q: Name the three parts of the male urethra.
questions.explain: The membranous part passes through the urogenital diaphragm, where the external sphincter is found.

open.q: Name the three parts of the male urethra.

questions.q: Which receptors relax the detrusor during filling, and which contract the trigone and internal urethral sphincter?
options: Beta receptors relax detrusor; alpha receptors contract trigone and internal sphincter
Muscarinic receptors relax detrusor; nicotinic receptors contract sphincter
Alpha receptors relax detrusor; beta receptors contract trigone
questions.explain: Noradrenaline from the hypogastric nerves (upper lumbar segments) acts on these receptors, so the bladder stores urine and the outlet stays closed.

open.q: Which receptors relax the detrusor during filling, and which contract the trigone and internal urethral sphincter?
accept: beta relax the detrusor, alpha contract the sphincter

questions.q: Which receptor mediates contraction of the detrusor after parasympathetic stimulation?
questions.explain: Acetylcholine from pelvic nerves (S2 to S4) acts on M3 receptors. This is why anticholinergic drugs are used for an overactive bladder.

open.q: Which receptor mediates contraction of the detrusor after parasympathetic stimulation?

questions.q: Which non-adrenergic, non-cholinergic transmitter relaxes the trigone and internal sphincter during voiding?
questions.explain: Nitric oxide is made from L-arginine by neuronal nitric oxide synthase and acts through cyclic GMP.

open.q: Which non-adrenergic, non-cholinergic transmitter relaxes the trigone and internal sphincter during voiding?

questions.q: What is stress incontinence?
options: Leakage with sudden urgency because the detrusor is overactive
Leakage when abdominal pressure rises, as the urethral closure is weak
Leakage that happens only during sleep at night
Complete inability to pass urine with a full bladder
questions.explain: Coughing, sneezing and lifting raise bladder pressure above the urethral closing pressure.

open.q: What is stress incontinence?

questions.q: What causes urge incontinence?
options: Weakness of the urethral closure mechanism
Stones in the bladder blocking the outlet
questions.explain: Patients feel sudden urgency and frequency and leak before reaching a toilet.

open.q: What causes urge incontinence?

questions.q: Which drugs are used for an overactive bladder, and which receptors do they block?
questions.explain: Bladder contraction is mediated by muscarinic receptors, but oral anticholinergics often give limited benefit and cause systemic side effects such as dry mouth.

open.q: Which drugs are used for an overactive bladder, and which receptors do they block?

questions.q: Tabes dorsalis (syphilis) causes which bladder abnormality?
options: A hyperactive bladder from an overactive detrusor
An uninhibited neurogenic bladder from partial cord damage
An automatic bladder from damage above the sacral cord
An atonic (tabetic) bladder from loss of sensory fibres
questions.explain: Loss of stretch signals abolishes the micturition reflex, so the bladder fills, becomes overdistended and overflows. A crush injury to the sacral cord has the same effect.

open.q: Tabes dorsalis (syphilis) causes which bladder abnormality?

questions.q: Which abnormality results from partial damage to the spinal cord or brain stem that removes most inhibitory signals?
questions.explain: The micturition reflex fires too easily, giving frequent, uncontrolled voiding with small volumes.

open.q: Which abnormality results from partial damage to the spinal cord or brain stem that removes most inhibitory signals?

questions.q: A man with benign prostatic enlargement has difficulty initiating urination and a weak urinary stream. Which mechanical change most directly explains these symptoms?
options: Increased resistance at the bladder outlet due to compression of the prostatic urethra
Failure of the detrusor to receive parasympathetic innervation
Loss of sensation from the bladder due to pudendal nerve damage
Excessive relaxation of the external urethral sphincter
questions.explain: Enlargement of the prostate can compress the prostatic urethra, increasing outlet resistance and producing hesitancy and a weak stream.

questions.q: A patient with an overactive bladder is prescribed oxybutynin. Which action accounts for its therapeutic effect?
options: Stimulation of beta-3 receptors to relax the detrusor
Blockade of muscarinic receptors, reducing involuntary detrusor contractions
Stimulation of alpha-1 receptors in the bladder wall
questions.explain: Oxybutynin is an antimuscarinic drug. It reduces cholinergic stimulation of the detrusor and helps control urgency and urge incontinence.

questions.q: A patient with spinal cord injury above the sacral micturition centre initially develops urinary retention. After spinal shock resolves, reflex bladder emptying returns but voluntary control is absent. What best describes this bladder?
options: Atonic bladder due to destruction of sacral reflex arcs
Automatic bladder due to an intact sacral reflex centre disconnected from higher control
Uninhibited bladder due to isolated pudendal nerve injury
questions.explain: When the sacral reflex circuitry remains intact but is disconnected from supraspinal control, reflex or automatic emptying may return after spinal shock, without normal voluntary control.

questions.q: Following pelvic surgery, a patient develops urinary retention because parasympathetic fibres to the bladder have been damaged. Which functional deficit is most directly expected?
options: Inability to contract the detrusor effectively during voiding
Inability to relax the external urethral sphincter because it is smooth muscle
Excessive contraction of the detrusor during bladder filling
Loss of sympathetic control of renal filtration
questions.explain: Pelvic parasympathetic nerves (S2–S4) provide the principal excitatory drive for detrusor contraction during micturition. Their injury can impair bladder emptying.

questions.q: A patient with spinal cord disease has impaired voluntary control of the external urethral sphincter but preserved detrusor contraction. Which nerve carries the somatic motor supply to this sphincter?
questions.explain: The external urethral sphincter is striated muscle supplied by somatic fibres in the pudendal nerve, arising from S2–S4.
